meta.title: TuxPress · empty repo to production
meta.outro: TuxPress is live · all checks green

events.text:
Build TuxPress — a Markdown-first publishing platform for developer teams.
Marketing site: hero, features, pricing, FAQ, footer. Dark, terminal-inspired, but clean.
App: magic-link auth, dashboard with posts list, Markdown editor with preview, publish/unpublish, settings.
Backend: Next.js App Router + TypeScript, Postgres via Drizzle, zod validation, rate limiting, health endpoint.
Tests: Vitest for units, Playwright for the main flows. CI: lint, typecheck, unit, e2e, build on every push.
Deploy when green. Use the existing empty repo and make it production-ready.

The repository only contains a README and an Apache-2.0 license, so there is no existing architecture to preserve. I'll pick a boring, production-friendly stack: Next.js App Router with TypeScript, Tailwind v4 for the design system, Drizzle + Postgres for persistence, Better Auth for magic links, and Vitest/Playwright for verification. Keeping everything in one deployable app removes an unnecessary API boundary for a product at this stage.
2 │ An empty cli for lazy developers. Just some random TUX

events.text: Route groups will keep the public site and the dashboard independent while sharing one layout: `(marketing)` for SEO pages, `(auth)` for login, `(dashboard)` for the app. API routes live under `src/app/api`. Shared primitives go under `src/components/ui`, and all database access stays in server-only modules so credentials never reach the client bundle.

2. Ship the marketing site behind a tiny design system.
3. Add Postgres, Drizzle migrations and magic-link auth.
4. Build dashboard CRUD plus the Markdown editor.
5. Lock the flows with Vitest + Playwright, then wire CI and deploy.

Starting with the scaffold. I'll keep a green build after each layer.

events.text: The dependency tree is small enough to reason about: 47 runtime packages and 38 dev-only packages, with no audit findings. The lockfile is the contract I care about. I'll commit it with the scaffold and let CI install with `--frozen-lockfile`, so a green build in Actions cannot silently resolve a different tree than the one I tested.

baseline build green · 2 static routes · no warnings

The baseline is green with five static routes and no warnings. I'm choosing the App Router without a separate API server because server components can query Postgres directly and the route handlers cover the browser-facing mutations. Route groups will keep the marketing shell, auth shell and dashboard shell visually independent while sharing one root layout.

The landing page should feel terminal-native without becoming a gimmick. I'll use a near-black canvas, a single cyan accent, Geist Mono for labels and Geist Sans for prose. The hero gets one strong promise and a live-looking product frame; the feature grid explains outcomes rather than implementation. Motion stays subtle and respects `prefers-reduced-motion`.

The token layer uses OKLab color mixing for borders, which keeps the dark surfaces from looking flat without introducing a second palette. I chose one accent and let contrast do the hierarchy work. I'll check the focus ring and placeholder contrast during the visual audit; those are the two places where terminal-inspired themes usually fail accessibility.

The CSP is the riskiest production change because it can break the app only after deploy. Next.js injects inline bootstrap scripts, so `script-src 'unsafe-inline'` stays for now; a nonce-based policy is a follow-up that needs middleware wiring. Everything else is locked down: no framing, no object embedding, same-origin forms, and a 2-year HSTS header. I'll verify the headers on the preview before promoting.

The marketing surface is now complete enough to be judged: social proof, a real blog index, legal pages, status, changelog, manifest, OG image, sitemap and RSS. The next risk is no longer visual; it is data integrity. Posts have no revision history yet, so a bad publish would overwrite the previous body with no recovery path. That is worth fixing before tests.

The marketing surface is in place: hero, social proof, six feature cards, a four-step workflow, testimonials, three pricing tiers, an FAQ accordion and a final CTA. The mobile audit caught one overflow issue in the hero, now fixed. I also added the public pages a real launch needs: blog index, about, status, changelog, privacy, sitemap, RSS and a generated OG image. Next I'll connect the database and auth layers so the dashboard is real rather than a mock.

▸ Todo 4/9 · Model database schema and migrations

Posts need a stable public identity and a private editorial workflow. A UUID primary key keeps references safe, while a unique slug is the public handle. Status is an enum-like text column with a check constraint added in the migration. Published posts also store `publishedAt` so the marketing site can order by real publication time. I'll index (status, published_at) to keep the public feed cheap.

The schema intentionally stores status as text with an enum in TypeScript and a check constraint in the migration. That keeps reads simple while still rejecting bad writes. The feed index is `(status, published_at)` because the public query always filters published and orders by date; a slug-only index would force a sort after the filter. I'll verify the plan later with `EXPLAIN`, but the shape is right.

The migration is additive, so rollback is a matter of dropping three empty tables rather than reversing data changes. I still want a forward-only habit in CI: generate the SQL, review it, apply it, then let the app build. `drizzle-kit push` is convenient locally, but the production path will use the generated file so the database change is visible in code review.

Magic links avoid password storage and are a good fit for developer teams. Better Auth can own users, sessions and verification tokens through the Drizzle adapter. The dashboard is protected in middleware; API handlers still re-check the session because middleware is not a security boundary. E2E tests will seed a session through a test-only helper gated by `NODE_ENV !== 'production'`.

Auth is the highest-risk surface, so I'm keeping the configuration boring: one adapter, one plugin, explicit trusted origins and a short cookie cache. The session cookie is httpOnly and same-site by default. The email sender suppresses delivery in tests and when no Resend key exists, which lets the app boot locally without pretending an email was sent.

The API contract is deliberately small: cursor pagination on `createdAt`, zod at the boundary, and explicit 401/422/429 responses. One subtle choice is generating the slug from the title inside the same request that inserts the post. That is not race-free under concurrent writes, but the unique index is the real guard; a future retry can turn a 23505 into a suffixed slug. I'll note it rather than over-engineer a locking path now.

One type error remains: `nextCursor` is a Date or null, but `NextResponse.json` infers a narrower shape from the sliced array. The clean fix is to serialize it explicitly to ISO instead of leaking a Date into the response contract. That also makes the cursor stable across runtimes.

Dashboard UX is intentionally table-first. The overview answers 'how much have I shipped?', the posts table answers 'what is the state of each post?', and the editor keeps the preview next to the source.
